questions.stem: An 88 year old woman with frailty and dementia is found by her carer sitting in her armchair in the morning. The heating has broken and it is January. She is drowsy and confused and her skin is cold. Her core temperature is 33.4°C, pulse rate 56 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg and respiratory rate 10 breaths per minute. Capillary glucose is 5.6 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A core temperature below 35°C is hypothermia, and frail elderly people with cold exposure are most at risk. A normal glucose excludes hypoglycaemia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Elderly, frail, **cold exposure**, confusion, slow breathing and a **core temperature below 35°C**.

elim: Her capillary glucose is normal.
Can cause hypothermia, but the clear cold exposure is the more likely cause and no thyroid history is given.
No opioid use or pinpoint pupils are described.
Possible in the elderly, but the cold house and core temperature point to environmental hypothermia.

steps.x: **B. Hypothermia.** Hypothermia = core temperature below 35°C; elderly patients are most prone.

questions.stem: A 32 year old roofer collapses after working all afternoon in direct sun on a hot day. He is confused. His temperature is 40.6°C, pulse rate 130 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg. He has no cough, urinary symptoms, rash or neck stiffness. He is given 1 g of intravenous paracetamol, but an hour later his temperature is unchanged.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the lack of response to paracetamol?
o: Failure of thermoregulation with a normal hypothalamic set point
questions.e: Hyperthermia is a failure of thermoregulation, not a raised hypothalamic set point as in fever, so paracetamol does not lower it. He needs rapid active cooling.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely explanation for the lack of response to paracetamol? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: working all afternoon in direct sun
no cough, urinary symptoms, rash or neck stiffness
steps.x: Heat exposure, no infective source, and **no response to antipyretics**.

elim: No neck stiffness, rash or headache is described, and infection would usually respond partly to antipyretics.
Fever raises the hypothalamic set point and usually responds to antipyretics.
Not a recognised cause of hyperthermia.
No thyroid history, goitre or eye signs, and the heat exposure explains the picture.

steps.x: **B. Failure of thermoregulation with a normal hypothalamic set point.** Hyperthermia is failure of thermoregulation, distinct from fever; antipyretics do not work.

questions.stem: An 83 year old man is admitted confused during a heatwave. He lives alone in a top floor flat and takes furosemide. He had drunk very little because he did not feel thirsty. His temperature is 40.3°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg. His skin is hot and dry.
questions.q: Which factor most increased his risk of this condition?
o: Impaired heat dissipation and reduced thirst with age
Living alone in a cold climate
questions.e: Older adults are at higher risk of heat stroke because of impaired heat dissipation and reduced thirst perception, often worsened by drugs such as diuretics. Sweating falls with age.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which factor most increased his risk of this condition? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
An older adult in a **heatwave** who **did not feel thirsty**, on a diuretic.

elim: Older adults have less muscle, and this is not a risk factor.
Sweating falls, not rises, with age.
He was exposed to heat, not cold.
That describes fever, not hyperthermia.

steps.x: **A. Impaired heat dissipation and reduced thirst with age.** Older adults have impaired heat dissipation and reduced thirst perception.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man collapses near the finish of a summer half marathon. Two runners nearby have been sweating heavily and feel faint but are alert. He is agitated, disorientated and his skin is hot and dry. His rectal temperature is 41.2°C, pulse rate 142 bpm and BP 98/56 mmHg.

visual.title: Core temperature
visual.label: 41.2°C
visual.caption: Above 40°C with confusion is heat stroke.

questions.q: Which feature most strongly indicates heat stroke in this runner?
o: Confusion with a core temperature above 40°C
Temperature of 38.5°C with normal mental state
questions.e: Heat stroke is defined by a core temperature above 40°C with CNS dysfunction, often with hot dry skin and absent sweating. Young active people are prone through exertion.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which feature most strongly indicates heat stroke in this runner? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: collapses near the finish of a summer half marathon
steps.x: A young, active person with **CNS dysfunction** and core temperature **above 40°C**.

elim: Common with simple dehydration or heat exhaustion.
Sweating continues in milder heat illness; in heat stroke sweating is often lost.
Tachycardia is common after any exercise.
Too low, and the mental state is normal.

steps.x: **A. Confusion with a core temperature above 40°C.** Heat stroke = core temperature above 40°C with CNS dysfunction, hot dry skin and loss of sweating.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man is found by a dog walker after falling in a park on a winter evening. He has been on the ground for about 3 hours. He is alert but a little confused. His core temperature is 33.8°C, pulse rate 68 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg and respiratory rate 12 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: Mild hypothermia causes shivering, cold skin, confusion and slow breathing. Hot dry skin is a feature of heat stroke.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on examination? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: on the ground for about 3 hours
steps.x: **Mild hypothermia** after cold exposure.

elim: Suggests serotonin syndrome.
Seen in sympathomimetic or serotonergic toxicity.
A sign of heat stroke.
Suggests opioid toxicity.

steps.x: **E. Shivering with cold, pale skin.** Hypothermia: shivering, confusion, cold skin and slow respirations; shivering is lost when severe.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman is found at home with a core temperature of 29.8°C. She is drowsy. Her pulse rate is 42 bpm and BP 92/56 mmHg. An ECG is recorded (see item resources). It shows sinus bradycardia with a positive deflection at the junction of the QRS complex and ST segment.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG on arrival
visual.caption: Sinus bradycardia with J (Osborn) waves at the end of the QRS, typical of hypothermia.

questions.q: Which other finding is most likely on this ECG?
o: Delta waves with a short PR interval
ST elevation in V1 to V4
questions.e: Hypothermia slows cardiac conduction, giving bradycardia, a prolonged QT and J (Osborn) waves. Hypercalcaemia shortens the QT.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which other finding is most likely on this ECG? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: junction of the QRS complex and ST segment
steps.x: Hypothermia with bradycardia and a **J (Osborn) wave**.

elim: Indicate an accessory pathway such as Wolff-Parkinson-White.
Suggest hyperkalaemia.
Seen in hypercalcaemia; cold lengthens the QT.
Suggests an anterior myocardial infarction.

steps.x: **C. Prolonged QT interval.** Hypothermia ECG: bradycardia, long QT and J waves, because cold slows conduction.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman takes sertraline for depression and was started on tramadol for back pain 2 days ago. She is agitated and confused with a tremor. It is a cool day and she has been indoors. Her temperature is 39.8°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 150/90 mmHg. Her pupils are dilated, reflexes are brisk and she has inducible ankle clonus.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her raised temperature?
questions.e: Serotonin syndrome causes hyperthermia with confusion, tremor, brisk reflexes and dilated pupils; here sertraline and tramadol interact. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome causes rigidity with reduced reflexes.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her raised temperature? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: cool day and she has been indoors
steps.x: Two **serotonergic drugs**, hyperthermia **without heat exposure**, tremor, brisk reflexes, clonus and dilated pupils.

elim: There is no environmental heat exposure or exertion.
No headache, rash or neck stiffness, and it does not cause clonus.
Follows antipsychotics, with rigidity, slow onset and reduced reflexes.
No thyroid history, and it does not cause clonus with brisk reflexes.

steps.x: **D. Serotonin syndrome.** Hyperthermia without environmental heat: think serotonin syndrome or MDMA.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man works in a hot foundry. He becomes confused at the end of his shift and his colleagues bring him to the Emergency Department. His temperature is 40.5°C, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and BP 108/64 mmHg. He has been vomiting.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: Hyperthermia causes a high temperature, confusion, hot skin and tachycardia, progressing to seizures and multi-organ failure. Bradycardia with cold skin is hypothermia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on examination? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: confused at the end of his shift
steps.x: Environmental heat with **confusion** and a very high temperature: hyperthermia.

elim: Features of hypothermia.
Cushing's reflex from raised intracranial pressure.
Suggests opioid toxicity.
A heat-producing response seen in cold exposure.

steps.x: **B. Hot skin with tachycardia.** Hyperthermia: high temperature, confusion, hot skin and tachycardia; severe = seizures and organ failure.

questions.stem: A 20 year old student is found asleep on a park bench at 4 am in February after a night out. He smells strongly of alcohol. He is drowsy and slurring his words. His core temperature is 32.6°C, pulse rate 54 bpm, BP 104/64 mmHg and respiratory rate 10 breaths per minute. His pupils are normal in size. Capillary glucose is 4.9 mmol/L and CT head is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his reduced consciousness, alongside alcohol?
questions.e: Alcohol and cold exposure are risk factors for hypothermia, which causes reduced consciousness and bradycardia. Normal glucose, pupils and CT exclude the other options.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his reduced consciousness, alongside alcohol? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: park bench at 4 am in February
steps.x: **Alcohol** plus **cold exposure** with a core temperature below 35°C.

elim: His glucose is normal.
CT head is normal.
His pupils are normal in size.
No seizure activity is described.

steps.x: **B. Hypothermia.** Risk factors for both conditions: environmental exposure, drugs, alcohol, frailty.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man is brought in after a night outdoors in freezing weather. His core temperature is 27.4°C. He is unresponsive, not shivering, with a pulse rate of 34 bpm and BP 74/40 mmHg. The paramedic warns the team to move him gently.
questions.q: Which arrhythmia is he at greatest risk of developing?
questions.e: Severe hypothermia slows conduction and makes the myocardium irritable, predisposing to VF, which may be triggered by rough handling and is often refractory until the patient is rewarmed.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which arrhythmia is he at greatest risk of developing? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Severe hypothermia** with bradycardia: the cold myocardium is irritable.

elim: Not the main danger with rough handling in severe hypothermia.
Cold slows, rather than speeds, conduction.
Not the classic risk here.
Needs an accessory pathway.

steps.x: **D. Ventricular fibrillation.** Severe hypothermia predisposes to VF, which is often refractory to defibrillation until rewarmed.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman collapses in an air-conditioned nightclub. Her friend says she took two pills earlier. She is agitated and sweating with jaw clenching. Her temperature is 40.1°C, pulse rate 140 bpm and BP 162/98 mmHg. Her pupils are dilated and her reflexes are brisk. Sodium is 128 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her hyperthermia?
questions.e: MDMA causes hyperthermia with agitation, jaw clenching, dilated pupils, brisk reflexes and often hyponatraemia. In an air-conditioned room, environmental heat stroke is less likely.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her hyperthermia? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Hyperthermia **without environmental heat** after pills, with jaw clenching, dilated pupils and low sodium.

elim: The club is air-conditioned, and the pills, jaw clenching and dilated pupils point to a drug cause.
Causes pinpoint pupils, slow breathing and low temperature.
No rash or neck stiffness, and the drug history explains it.
Needs an antipsychotic and causes rigidity with reduced reflexes.

steps.x: **C. MDMA toxicity.** Consider MDMA or serotonin syndrome when hyperthermia occurs without clear heat exposure.

questions.stem: An 84 year old man is brought in from his garden shed on a cold morning. He is drowsy and his skin is cold. A tympanic thermometer reads 35.6°C, but the nurse thinks he feels much colder. His pulse rate is 46 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm his temperature?
o: Core temperature with an oesophageal probe
questions.e: Core temperature measured with an oesophageal (or bladder) probe is the gold standard. Tympanic, oral and skin readings are unreliable in hypothermia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm his temperature? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Peripheral readings **underestimate** cold; you need **core** temperature.

elim: Peripheral and unreliable when the patient is cold.
Measures skin temperature, which is unreliable in hypothermia.
Peripheral and unreliable in a drowsy, cold patient.
Tympanic readings are unreliable in hypothermia.

steps.x: **B. Core temperature with an oesophageal probe.** Gold standard: core temperature with a bladder or oesophageal probe.

questions.stem: A 90 year old woman is found on her kitchen floor in a cold house. Her core temperature is 31.2°C and she is drowsy. Her pulse rate is 48 bpm and BP 100/58 mmHg. Warming blankets are being applied.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial blood test?
questions.e: U&Es and glucose are first-line in both hypothermia and hyperthermia; CK is added in hyperthermia to look for rhabdomyolysis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial blood test? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Hypothermia: check for **glucose** and **electrolyte** problems that change management.

elim: May be needed if sepsis is suspected, but not instead of electrolytes and glucose.
Added in hyperthermia for rhabdomyolysis, not the first-line test here.
Not a first-line test in hypothermia.
May find a cause later but are not the initial test.

steps.x: **E. Urea, electrolytes and glucose.** First-line in both conditions: U&Es and glucose; add CK in hyperthermia.

questions.stem: A 24 year old soldier is treated for exertional heat stroke. His temperature was 41.6°C and he is now cooled. His urine is dark brown. His creatine kinase is 52,000 U/L (25–200).
questions.q: Which result on urea and electrolytes is most likely?
o: Normal creatinine and low sodium only
questions.e: Heat stroke causes rhabdomyolysis, releasing potassium and myoglobin, which causes acute kidney injury with a raised creatinine and hyperkalaemia. U&Es and CK are first-line in hyperthermia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which result on urea and electrolytes is most likely? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Heat stroke has caused **rhabdomyolysis**: muscle contents leak and myoglobin damages the kidneys.

elim: Muscle breakdown raises both.
Does not fit rhabdomyolysis with dark urine.
Muscle cells release potassium, so it rises.
Does not reflect the kidney injury from myoglobin.

steps.x: **D. Raised creatinine and raised potassium.** CK is added in hyperthermia to look for rhabdomyolysis; check U&Es for AKI and hyperkalaemia.

questions.stem: An 81 year old man is admitted with a core temperature of 30.4°C. He is drowsy, his pulse rate is 40 bpm and BP 94/56 mmHg. Warmed intravenous fluids and forced-air warming are started.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional investigation?
o: Continuous cardiac monitoring and a 12-lead ECG
questions.e: Hypothermia causes bradycardia, a long QT, J waves and a risk of VF, so cardiac monitoring and a 12-lead ECG are needed alongside rewarming.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate additional investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Moderate hypothermia with **bradycardia**: high risk of arrhythmia.

elim: Not routinely needed without a head injury or focal signs.
Not the urgent test for hypothermia-related arrhythmias.
Only if CNS infection is suspected.
Not relevant to his acute condition.

steps.x: **A. Continuous cardiac monitoring and a 12-lead ECG.** Supportive care in both: warmed IV fluids and cardiac monitoring; ECG shows bradycardia, long QT, J waves.

questions.stem: A 20 year old woman took MDMA at a festival and was treated for hyperthermia with a peak temperature of 40.8°C. She is now cooled and alert, but her muscles ache and she has passed dark urine. Urine dipstick shows blood 3+ but microscopy shows no red cells. U&Es and glucose have been sent.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional investigation?
questions.e: Hyperthermia can cause rhabdomyolysis, and myoglobin makes the dipstick positive for blood without red cells, so CK is added to U&Es and glucose. Cystoscopy looks for bladder bleeding.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate additional investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: blood 3+ but microscopy shows no red cells
steps.x: Dipstick blood **without red cells** = myoglobin from muscle breakdown.

elim: Investigates bladder bleeding; there are no red cells in the urine.
Looks for obstruction, not muscle breakdown.
Tests for pancreatitis.
Looks for infection, which does not explain blood on dipstick without red cells.

steps.x: **D. Serum creatine kinase.** In hyperthermia, add creatine kinase to U&Es and glucose to look for rhabdomyolysis.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman is found at home after lying on the floor overnight. Her core temperature is 30.2°C. She is drowsy and not shivering. Her pulse rate is 44 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg. She has a pulse and is breathing.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Active rewarming with warmed intravenous fluids and forced-air warming
Hot water bottles to the limbs
questions.e: Severe hypothermia needs active rewarming with warmed IV fluids and forced-air warming blankets, plus cardiac monitoring. Passive rewarming alone is for mild hypothermia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Severe hypothermia** with a pulse, above 28°C.

elim: Peripheral heating can cause vasodilation and burns, and is not an appropriate active method.
She has a pulse and is not in VF.
Used for mild hypothermia; she is severely cold and not shivering.
Reserved for temperatures below 28°C with cardiovascular instability or arrest.

steps.x: **A. Active rewarming with warmed intravenous fluids and forced-air warming.** Mild = passive external rewarming; severe = active rewarming with warmed IV fluids and forced-air blankets.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has a 3 hour open bowel resection. In recovery his core temperature is 35.1°C. He is drowsy from anaesthesia and shivering. His pulse rate is 62 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate method of rewarming?
o: Radiant heat lamp to the head only
questions.e: Forced-air (heated air) warming blankets are the primary method of rewarming perioperative patients. Invasive methods such as ECMO or peritoneal lavage are only for severe hypothermia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate method of rewarming? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Perioperative** hypothermia after a long operation.

elim: Would cool him further.
Reserved for severe hypothermia below 28°C with instability.
Invasive; reserved for severe hypothermia when ECMO is not available.
Not an effective way to rewarm a perioperative patient.

steps.x: **C. Forced-air warming blanket.** Forced-air warming blankets are the primary perioperative rewarming method.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man with exertional heat stroke is being cooled by cold water immersion. His temperature has fallen from 41.4°C to 39.2°C. He remains tachycardic at 126 bpm with BP 100/58 mmHg and his mucous membranes are dry. He is drowsy and cannot drink safely.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional management?
questions.e: Heat stroke is treated with rapid active cooling combined with rehydration, which here must be intravenous because he cannot drink safely. Antipyretics do not work in hyperthermia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate additional management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Cooling is under way; he is still **dehydrated** and **cannot drink**.

elim: Used for malignant hyperthermia after anaesthesia, not exertional heat stroke.
Antipyretics do not work in hyperthermia and he cannot swallow safely.
He cannot drink safely.
He is still above the target; continue until about 38 to 39°C and give fluids.

steps.x: **B. Intravenous fluid rehydration.** Combine rapid active cooling with oral or IV rehydration.

questions.stem: An 89 year old woman with heart failure is brought in during a heatwave. She is confused with a temperature of 40.4°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 104/60 mmHg. She is frail and has a pressure sore, so cold water immersion is not practical.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Ice packs to the groin, axillae and neck with fans and water spray
Passive cooling in a cool room only
questions.e: Heat stroke needs rapid active cooling; when immersion is not practical, ice packs to the groin, axillae and neck with fans and cold water spray are used. Antipyretics do not work.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: cold water immersion is not practical
steps.x: **Heat stroke** in a frail patient who cannot be immersed.

elim: Used for malignant hyperthermia, not heat stroke.
Antipyretics do not work in hyperthermia.
Too slow for heat stroke.
Used for hypothermia, and would add heat.

steps.x: **A. Ice packs to the groin, axillae and neck with fans and water spray.** Rapid active cooling first-line: ice packs to groin, axillae and neck, cold water immersion, fans and spray.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man is found in the snow. His core temperature is 25.8°C and his GCS is 6. His pulse rate is 30 bpm and BP 68/36 mmHg. He is in a district general hospital that has no ECMO service, and transfer will take several hours.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate method of rewarming?
questions.e: Severe hypothermia below 28°C with impaired consciousness, bradycardia and hypotension needs ECMO; when ECMO is unavailable, peritoneal lavage with warmed saline is used instead.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate method of rewarming? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Below 28°C** with instability, ECMO is first choice, but it is **not available**.

elim: Too slow for severe hypothermia with cardiovascular instability.
Risks rewarming shock and arrhythmias and is impractical with a GCS of 6.
Only for mild hypothermia.
Peripheral and too slow.

steps.x: **D. Peritoneal lavage with warmed saline.** Severe hypothermia below 28°C: ECMO; if unavailable, peritoneal lavage with warmed saline.

questions.stem: A 81 year old woman with severe hypothermia is being actively rewarmed. Her core temperature has risen from 28.5°C to 32.0°C over 2 hours. Her BP falls from 104/62 to 76/40 mmHg, her pulse rate is 98 bpm and her peripheries are now warm. Her chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Rewarming causes peripheral vasodilation without a matching rise in cardiac output, causing distributive (rewarming) shock. It is treated with warmed IV fluids while rewarming continues.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
BP falls as she **warms** and her **peripheries dilate**: rewarming shock.

elim: She has a perfusing rhythm.
Would worsen the hypotension.
She is still hypothermic.
Rewarming must continue; the shock is treated with fluid.

steps.x: **E. Warmed intravenous fluid bolus.** Rapid rewarming causes peripheral vasodilation and distributive shock; treat with warmed IV fluid.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man is in cardiac arrest after falling into a cold canal. He has had three shocks for ventricular fibrillation at a core temperature of 27.0°C, without success, followed by CPR and active rewarming. His core temperature is now 30.6°C and he remains in ventricular fibrillation.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Give a fourth shock only after 37°C
questions.e: Resuscitation Council UK guidance is up to 3 shocks in hypothermic arrest, then no further shocks until the core temperature is above 30°C. He has reached it, so defibrillation can resume.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Three shocks given while cold; now **rewarmed above 30°C**.

elim: Shocks can be resumed once the core temperature reaches 30°C.
Too late; 30°C is the threshold.
CPR must continue in hypothermic arrest.
Hypothermic patients should not be declared dead until rewarmed.

steps.x: **D. Resume defibrillation.** Hypothermic arrest: up to 3 shocks, then no more until the core temperature is above 30°C.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman on citalopram and recently started on linezolid is agitated with a tremor and brisk reflexes. Her temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 122 bpm and BP 148/92 mmHg. Her pupils are dilated. She has not been exposed to heat. She is being given intravenous fluids and cooled.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Serotonin syndrome is treated by stopping the offending serotonergic drugs alongside cooling and supportive care. Increasing the dose or adding tramadol would worsen it.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Hyperthermia from **serotonin syndrome** caused by two serotonergic drugs.

elim: Would worsen serotonin toxicity.
An antipsychotic that can worsen hyperthermia and is not the treatment.
Antipyretics do not treat drug-induced hyperthermia.
Another serotonergic drug.

steps.x: **E. Stop the citalopram and linezolid.** Always treat the underlying cause: stop the offending drug or remove from the heat source.

questions.stem: An 82 year old man is admitted with a core temperature of 34.2°C. He is alert and shivering. He has a productive cough and crackles at the right base. His pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. His chest X-ray shows right lower zone consolidation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Passive rewarming with blankets and antibiotics for pneumonia
questions.e: Mild hypothermia is treated with passive external rewarming, and the underlying cause, here pneumonia, must also be treated. Rewarming alone would leave the infection untreated.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Mild hypothermia** triggered by **infection**.

elim: A cooling treatment for heat stroke.
For severe hypothermia below 28°C with instability.
Warms him but leaves the infection causing his hypothermia untreated.
Invasive and for severe hypothermia only.

steps.x: **C. Passive rewarming with blankets and antibiotics for pneumonia.** Mild: passive external rewarming. Always treat the underlying cause.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man has surgery for a large craniopharyngioma. Afterwards his temperature swings between 34°C and 39°C depending on the room temperature. He does not shiver when cold or sweat when hot.
questions.q: Damage to which structure best explains his temperature instability?
questions.e: The hypothalamus controls body temperature by balancing heat production, such as shivering, and heat loss, such as sweating and vasodilation. Damage leaves temperature dependent on the environment.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Damage to which structure best explains his temperature instability? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: does not shiver when cold or sweat when hot
steps.x: Loss of **both** heat production and heat loss responses.

elim: Coordinates movement, not temperature.
Controls breathing and heart rate, not the temperature set point.
Secretes hormones but does not set body temperature.
Relays sensory information but does not regulate temperature.

steps.x: **B. Hypothalamus.** The hypothalamus balances heat production (shivering) and heat loss (sweating, vasodilation).

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with heat stroke has a core temperature of 41.0°C. His skin is hot and completely dry, though he had been sweating heavily earlier in the day. He is confused.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason his temperature has risen so high?
o: Loss of sweating as thermoregulation fails
Vasoconstriction of skin vessels to lose heat
questions.e: Heat stroke represents failure of thermoregulatory compensation: sweating stops, so heat cannot be lost by evaporation and core temperature rises. Fever involves a raised set point instead.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely reason his temperature has risen so high? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: sweating heavily earlier in the day
steps.x: Sweating has **stopped**: the main route of heat loss has failed.

elim: Shivering produces heat in the cold; it is not happening here.
That describes fever from infection.
Would lower, not raise, heat production.
Vasoconstriction conserves heat; vasodilation loses it.

steps.x: **B. Loss of sweating as thermoregulation fails.** Heat stroke is failure of thermoregulatory compensation with loss of sweating.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has a core temperature of 29.0°C. Her ECG shows sinus bradycardia with prominent J (Osborn) waves. A cardiology registrar explains that cold affects one ion current in the epicardium more than the endocardium.
questions.q: Which ion current change best explains the J wave?
o: Increased funny current in the sinoatrial node
Reduced sodium-potassium ATPase in red cells
